summary: Describes early DNS security extensions that add cryptographic digital signatures so resolvers and applications can verify DNS data integrity and authenticity. It was replaced by RFC 2535.

eli5.summary: The phone book entries get a seal that proves they are real. It was an early attempt at DNS sealing.

questions: what was the first dnssec specification
what is the sig record in dns
what does the nxt record do
subtitle: The first DNS security extensions: signed records, stored public keys and authenticated denial of existence.

tldr.problem: The DNS had become a critical part of Internet infrastructure but had no strong mechanism to assure data integrity or authentication.
tldr.mechanism: Zones carry digital signatures as SIG resource records, public keys as KEY records, and NXT records that sign the non-existence of names and types. Two new header bits, AD and CD, let resolvers and servers signal about verification.
tldr.outcome: This specification was a Proposed Standard but has been obsoleted by RFC 2535, so it is no longer the current DNS security definition.

today: RFC 2065 was a Proposed Standard but has been obsoleted by RFC 2535, which is the one to read for this design. It updated RFC 1034 and RFC 1035.

sections.title: What the Extensions Provide
sections.content:
RFC 2065 adds DNS security through cryptographic digital signatures stored in the zone as resource records. It provides three services: key distribution, data origin authentication with integrity, and optional transaction and request authentication. Security can still be provided through non-security aware servers in many cases.

The RFC is explicit about what it leaves out. The DNS treats its data as public and gives the same answers to all inquirers, so there are no access control lists, and no confidentiality for queries or responses (the RFC points to IPSEC for that).

Authentication normally uses one private key for the whole zone, kept off-line and used to re-sign all the records periodically. The key belongs to the zone and not to the servers that store copies, so compromising a server does not necessarily affect a resolver's ability to tell genuine data. A resolver learns a zone's public key by reading it from the DNS (where the key is itself signed) or by static configuration, so it must be configured with at least one starting key. The RFC updates RFC 1034 and RFC 1035.
sections.eli5: The DNS is like a public phone book. This adds a seal to each entry so you can tell the entry is real, but it does not hide who is asking.

sections.title: The KEY Record
sections.content:
The KEY resource record (type 25) ties a public key to a DNS name. Its data holds a 16-bit flags field, a protocol octet, an algorithm number and the key itself. The key can belong to a zone, a host or other end entity, or a user, and the flags say which. Implementations MUST handle at least two simultaneously valid keys of the same type for a name.

The flags include a type field (bits 0 and 1) that can mark a key as prohibited for authentication or confidentiality, or, with both bits set, the "no key" value that lets a signed KEY record assert that a zone is not secured. Other bits mark an experimental key, a user key (bit 5), an entity key (bit 6) and a zone key (bit 7), and bits 12 to 15 form a signatory field.

Algorithm 1 is MD5/RSA. Numbers 2 through 252 are available for assignment, 253 is the "expiration date algorithm", and 254 is for private use with an OID. For MD5/RSA the exponent and modulus are each limited to 2552 bits.
sections.eli5: A KEY record is a name tag on a locked mailbox slot: it says whose public lock this is and what kind of thing owns it, such as a zone, a computer or a person.

sections.title: The SIG Record
sections.content:
The SIG resource record (type 24) is the heart of the scheme. It signs all records of one type, class and name and binds them to a time interval and to the signer's domain name. Its data holds the type covered, the algorithm, a labels count, the original TTL, a signature expiration time, the time signed, a 16-bit key footprint, the signer's name and the signature.

The original TTL is signed, while the current TTL is not. This lets caches count the TTL down without breaking the signature, and a security aware resolver limits the TTL it uses to the original signed value. To sign, the data is the SIG's own fields before the signature followed by the covered records in canonical form: names fully expanded, lower case, original TTL, and sorted by name, type and data. For MD5/RSA the hash is MD5 over this data, wrapped in the format of PKCS1, and the modulus must be from 512 to 2552 bits.

Special SIGs have a type covered of zero. A server can add one at the end of a response, signed with the server's host key, to authenticate the transaction (it covers the response plus the query). A request can carry one too. A zone transfer can carry an AXFR SIG that covers the whole zone. A transaction SIG does not authenticate any records itself.
sections.eli5: A SIG record is the wax seal. It says who sealed the entry, when the seal starts to count, and when it runs out.

sections.title: Proving a Name or Type Does Not Exist
sections.content:
Signatures only protect records that exist, so the NXT record (type 30) is added to sign the gaps. An NXT record has an existing name as its owner. Its data is the next name in the zone's canonical order plus a bit map showing which record types exist at the owner name. Together they say that no name falls between the two, and that no other signed types exist at the owner name.

The last NXT in a zone holds the zone name, so the name space is treated as circular. A server that gets a query for a missing name returns the NXT and its SIG in the authority section along with the error.

The RFC points out a side effect: a resolver can follow the next-name fields from one NXT to the next and so walk through the whole zone, defeating attempts to block zone transfers. Wildcards complicate the picture, since a malicious server could hide more specific names behind a wildcard NXT.
sections.eli5: To prove a name is not in the book, the book shows two neighbors and a seal saying nothing sits between them.

sections.title: AD and CD Bits and Secure Resolution
sections.content:
Two previously unused header bits are taken from the must-be-zero Z field. The AD (authentic data) bit says in a response that the server has verified the data. The CD (checking disabled) bit says in a query that unverified data is acceptable. Old servers and resolvers leave both at zero, so security aware servers answer them only with authenticated data. A security aware resolver SHOULD set CD to cut latency, and MUST NOT trust the AD bit unless it trusts the server and has a secure path to it or uses transaction security.

Servers hold data as Authenticated, Pending or Insecure, plus a transient Bad state that is never kept. A server never returns Bad data. A resolver starts from configured trusted keys, added with a pubkey boot file directive, and chains through zones. It keeps a distance count of secure zones traversed, and it should refuse to step from a secure zone into a non-secure one unless a KEY record certifies that zone as non-secure or experimental. Time must also be kept consistent and secure, since signatures have timestamps.
sections.eli5: Two little flags on each question and answer tell everyone whether the seals have been checked yet and whether the asker wants to skip checking.

sections.title: Operations and Security Limits
sections.content:
The RFC recommends keeping zone private keys and the master zone file on off-line machines that are not on the network, adding SIG and NXT records periodically and then moving the file to the primary server. Non-zone keys generally must stay on-line. Key generation should also be off-line. It suggests no zone key lifetime significantly over four years, with 13 months as a reasonable maximum for off-line zone keys, and 36 days for on-line entity and user keys.

On key size, the recommended minimum RSA modulus is 640 bits, and the RFC says larger keys enlarge KEY and SIG records and raise the chance of UDP packet overflow. Servers and resolvers each have minimal and full conformance levels, and a primary server for a secure zone MUST be fully compliant.

The Security Considerations are modest. The extensions guarantee at most the validity of resource records retrieved from the DNS. They do not stop someone from substituting an unauthorized host at an address that secure DNS returned correctly.
sections.eli5: Keep the stamp that makes the seals locked away from the internet, change it regularly, and remember a real seal only proves an entry is genuine, not that the place it points to is safe.

items.label: Type
items.desc: Prohibits use for authentication or confidentiality; both set means no key.

items.label: Experimental
items.desc: Key is for experimental, trial or optional use.

items.label: User
items.desc: Key belongs to a user or account.

items.label: Entity
items.desc: Key belongs to a non-zone entity, commonly a host.

items.label: Zone
items.desc: Zone key used for DNS data origin authentication.

items.label: IPSEC
items.desc: Reserved; key is valid for use with IPSEC.

items.label: Email
items.desc: Reserved; key is valid for MIME security multiparts.

items.label: Signatory
items.desc: If non-zero, the key can validly sign records or updates of the same name.
